weeks.title: Fractions and equal parts
weeks.big_idea: The whole stays the same when fractions are compared. Multiplication can take part of an amount. Division can count fractional groups or split a fraction into shares.
weeks.connections: This builds on equal sharing and multiplication facts. Next, ratios compare amounts that change together.
weeks.omissions: The diagnostic samples Grade 5 rather than reteaching every standard. General fraction division waits until Week 4; unlike-denominator addition and subtraction recur in practice.

teaser.text: A card shows a fraction. Its denominator is 8. It lies between {1/2} and {3/4}. What fraction is on the card?
teaser.worked: Half is four eighths and three fourths is six eighths. Only five eighths lies strictly between them.

sessions.title: Fractions on one number line
sessions.goal: I can compare fractions and decimals by placing them on the same number line.
sessions.key_idea: A fraction names equal parts of one whole. The size of that whole stays fixed.
sessions.prerequisite: Name numerator and denominator. Divide a whole into equal parts.

vocab.meaning: The top number counts equal parts.
The bottom number names how many equal parts make one whole.
Different names for the same amount.
The result of division.

problems.text: Compare {3/7} and {5/7}. Write <, >, or =.
problems.worked: Both use sevenths. Three parts are fewer than five.
problems.error: Counting denominator size instead of the number of parts.

problems.text: Compare {4/5} and {4/9}. Use strips of the same length.
problems.worked: Fifths are larger than ninths, so four fifths cover more.
problems.error: Thinking a larger denominator makes a larger amount.

problems.text: Is {5/12} less than or greater than {1/2}?
problems.worked: Half of twelve parts is six parts. Five twelfths is below half.

problems.text: Compare {3/5} and {7/12}. Rename both using sixtieths.
On a 0-to-2 line, place {5/4}, 1 {3/4}, and 0.5.
problems.case: Improper fraction, mixed number and decimal
problems.worked: {5/4} = 1 {1/4}. Split each whole into four equal steps.

diagram.caption: Each tick interval is one fourth.

problems.text: Compare {7/10} and 0.68.
problems.worked: {7/10} = 0.70, which is 2 hundredths more than 0.68.

problems.text: A line has ticks at 0, 2, and 4. Place 2 {1/2}.
problems.answer: One fourth of the way from 2 to 4
problems.worked: The interval from 2 to 4 is two units. Half a unit uses one fourth of that interval.

diagram.caption: Main ticks are two units apart.

problems.text: Three identical muffins are shared equally by four friends. How much muffin does each friend receive?
problems.worked: Split each muffin into fourths. Each friend gets three fourths.

exit.text: Order {3/4}, {7/10}, and 0.72 from least to greatest. Place them on a 0-to-1 line.
exit.worked: Rename as 0.70, 0.72, 0.75. Their positions increase to the right.
exit.error: The larger denominator does not make the fraction larger.

error.text: Nora says {4/9} is greater than {4/5} because 9 is greater than 5. Explain and repair her claim.
error.correction: {4/5} > {4/9}. Nine equal pieces are smaller than five equal pieces of the same whole.
error.why: She compares denominator counts without comparing piece sizes.
error.move: Align equal-length strips. Cover four fifths and four ninths.

steps: Use one whole for both fractions.
Split the whole into 12 equal parts.
Eight twelfths is less than nine twelfths.

model.caption: One whole keeps the same length.

look_fors.response: Uses equal-length wholes.
look_fors.why: Comparisons require the same unit.
look_fors.move: Ask the student to mark 0 and 1 on both strips.

look_fors.response: Uses a benchmark or common denominator.
look_fors.why: Both are valid comparison methods.
look_fors.move: Accept either method and ask where the fractions lie.

look_fors.response: Counts spaces between ticks, not tick marks.
look_fors.why: Each space represents an equal fractional step.
look_fors.move: Trace one interval and name its length.

misconceptions.why: Thinks all fractions are less than one.
misconceptions.move: Build four fourths, then add one fourth.

misconceptions.why: Confuses number of parts with part size.
misconceptions.move: Compare equal-length strips cut into fifths and ninths.

discussion: Agree or disagree: More pieces always means more muffin. Use the same whole to support your answer.
Partner compare: How does a benchmark comparison differ from renaming both fractions?
sessions.summary_frame: To compare fractions, I first keep ___ the same. Then I can ___.

exit_sort.got: Orders all three correctly and places them in order between 0.7 and 0.8, with {3/4} at 0.75.
exit_sort.almost: Order is correct, but a position or label is imprecise; explains that larger denominator means smaller equal parts.
exit_sort.reteach: Reverses the fractions because 10 exceeds 4, or uses inconsistent units.

sessions.title: Fraction operations with models
sessions.goal: I can use equal parts to explain fraction multiplication and two kinds of division.
sessions.key_idea: Multiplication can take part of an amount. Division can count groups or find the size of each share.

vocab.meaning: Multiplying an amount to change its size.
A fraction with numerator 1.
The result of multiplication.

problems.text: Five bags each hold {3/4} cup of seeds. How many cups altogether?
problems.worked: Five groups of three fourths make fifteen fourths.

problems.text: A rectangle is {3/5} meter long and {2/3} meter wide. Find its area using equal parts.
problems.worked: Divide a unit square into 5 columns and 3 rows. The overlap is 6 of 15 parts.

diagram.caption: The overlap covers 6 of 15 equal parts.

problems.text: Find {2/3} of 1 {1/2} cups.
problems.worked: Rename 1 {1/2} as {3/2}. Two thirds of three halves is two halves.

problems.text: Without multiplying first, compare {3/4} × 8 and {5/4} × 8 with 8. Then compute.
problems.worked: Three fourths takes less than all eight. Five fourths takes more than all eight.

problems.text: Three meters of ribbon are cut into {1/4}-meter pieces. How many pieces?
problems.case: Whole number divided by unit fraction
problems.worked: There are four fourths per meter. Three meters hold twelve fourths.

problems.text: A {1/4}-liter juice sample is shared equally among three cups. How much goes in each cup?
problems.case: Unit fraction divided by whole number
problems.worked: Split one fourth into three equal parts. Each is one twelfth of a liter.

problems.text: Write one story for 2 ÷ {1/5} and one for {1/5} ÷ 2. Solve both.
problems.answer: 10 groups; {1/10} in each share. Stories vary.
problems.worked: Example: cut 2 meters into fifth-meter pieces; share a fifth-meter piece equally between two people.

exit.text: A board is 5 meters long. Each shelf needs {1/2} meter. How many shelves can be cut?
exit.case: Exit: division by a number below one
exit.worked: Each meter contains two half-meters, so five meters contain ten.
exit.error: Multiplying by one half answers a different question.

error.text: Eli says 3 ÷ {1/4} = {3/4}, because division makes numbers smaller. Show why this fails.
error.correction: Twelve quarter-meter pieces fit in 3 meters.
error.why: He treats division by a fraction as multiplication by that fraction.
error.move: Make one meter from four quarter-meter pieces, then repeat three times.

steps: Split a whole into 3 equal columns and 4 equal rows.
Select 2 columns, then 3 fourths of those columns.

fade.text: A model has 4 columns and 3 rows. Shade {3/4}, then {2/3} of it. Complete __ × __ = __.

look_fors.response: Counts overlapping equal parts in the area model.
look_fors.why: The overlap represents multiplication.
look_fors.move: Ask what fraction of the entire unit square is shaded twice.

look_fors.response: Predicts shrinking for a factor below one.
look_fors.why: Connects computation to scaling.
look_fors.move: Ask for an estimate before calculation.

look_fors.response: Distinguishes number of pieces from piece size.
look_fors.why: These division situations have different units.
look_fors.move: Accept a tape or a story, but require units in the answer.

misconceptions.response: Says multiplication always increases an amount.
misconceptions.why: Uses only whole-number experience.
misconceptions.move: Take half of a familiar amount.

misconceptions.response: Uses the same answer for reversed division.
misconceptions.why: Does not identify what is known and unknown.
misconceptions.move: Label total amount, number of groups, and group size.

discussion: Agree or disagree: Taking three fourths of a cup gives more than one cup.
Partner compare: In the two ribbon stories, which question counts pieces and which finds their size?
sessions.summary_frame: When I divide, I first ask whether I need the number of ___ or the size of ___.

exit_sort.got: Gives 10 shelves and connects five meters to ten equal half-meter pieces.
exit_sort.almost: Gives 10 but cannot yet explain the unit or draw equal pieces.
exit_sort.reteach: Gives 2 {1/2} or claims the answer must be below 5.

bank.text: Compare {2/9} and {7/9}.
bank.worked: With ninths fixed, compare two parts and seven parts.
bank.error: The numerator counts the parts.

bank.text: Which is closer to 1: {7/8} or {4/5}?
bank.worked: The gaps from 1 are one eighth and one fifth. One eighth is smaller.

bank.text: Compare {5/8} and {3/5}.
bank.worked: Rename as twenty-five fortieths and twenty-four fortieths.
bank.error: Compare equal-sized parts, not the original denominator counts.

bank.text: Order {2/5}, 0.45, and {1/2} from least to greatest.
bank.worked: Rename two fifths as 0.40 and one half as 0.50.

bank.text: A number line uses quarters from 0 to 2. Where does {7/4} belong?
bank.worked: Four fourths reach 1. Three more fourths reach one and three fourths.

bank.text: A line marks 0, 3, and 6. How far from 3 toward 6 is 4 {1/2}?
bank.worked: The interval is 3 units. One and one half units is half of that interval.

bank.text: Five granola bars are shared equally among six children. How much does each get?
bank.worked: Split each bar into sixths and give each child five sixths.

bank.text: Compare {1/3} and {1/4}.
bank.worked: With the same numerator, the fraction with larger pieces is larger.
bank.error: A larger denominator makes smaller equal parts, not a larger fraction.

bank.worked: Rename both fractions with a common denominator. Add the counts of equal parts.
Rename both fractions with a common denominator. Subtract equal parts.

bank.text: Compare {2/4} and {2/5}.
bank.worked: With the same numerator, the fraction with larger pieces is larger.
bank.error: A larger denominator makes smaller equal parts, not a larger fraction.

bank.worked: Rename both fractions with a common denominator. Add the counts of equal parts.
An area model shows 12 of 20 equal parts, or three fifths.

bank.text: Find {3/5} of 1 {2/3} cups.
bank.worked: Rename one and two thirds as five thirds. Three fifths of five thirds is one.

bank.text: Is {2/3} × 9 smaller or larger than 9? Compute to check.
bank.worked: Two thirds takes less than all nine.

bank.text: Is {4/3} × 6 smaller or larger than 6? Compute to check.
bank.worked: Four thirds takes one whole six plus one third of six.

bank.text: Find both 4 ÷ {1/5} and {1/5} ÷ 4.
bank.worked: The first counts fifths in four. The second splits one fifth into four shares.
bank.error: Changing the order changes what is shared or counted.

bank.text: A garden is {4/5} meter by {5/6} meter. Find its area.
bank.worked: Multiply the two side lengths and simplify twenty thirtieths.

bank.text: Write a story for {1/6} ÷ 3 and solve it.
bank.worked: Example: share one sixth liter equally among three cups. Each gets one eighteenth liter.
Count two thirds for each whole-number group, then rename the result.

bank.text: How many {1/3}-meter pieces fit in 2 meters?
bank.worked: Each meter contains 3 equal pieces. Multiply by 2 meters.
bank.error: Multiplying by the divisor answers a different question.

bank.text: Share {1/3} liter equally among 2 cups. How much per cup?
bank.worked: Split the given fractional amount into the stated number of equal shares.
bank.error: Multiplying by the divisor answers a different question.

bank.worked: Count two thirds for each whole-number group, then rename the result.

bank.text: How many {1/4}-meter pieces fit in 3 meters?
bank.worked: Each meter contains 4 equal pieces. Multiply by 3 meters.
bank.error: Multiplying by the divisor answers a different question.

weeks.title: Ratios and matching amounts
weeks.big_idea: A ratio compares two amounts in a chosen order. Equivalent ratios scale both amounts together. Tables and double number lines keep matching amounts connected.
weeks.connections: This builds on equal groups and fraction comparison. Next, unit rates and percents describe one-unit and hundred-unit comparisons.
weeks.omissions: Ratio reasoning uses friendly two-quantity examples. Multi-stage mixtures and formal cross-multiplication are omitted.

teaser.text: A tile bag has red : blue = 3 : 2. The total is greater than 20 and less than 30. How many of each color?
teaser.worked: One batch contains five tiles. The only multiple of five strictly between 20 and 30 is 25.

sessions.title: Equivalent ratios
sessions.goal: I can keep a ratio unchanged while making more or less of a mixture.
sessions.key_idea: Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both quantities by the same factor.

vocab.meaning: A comparison of two amounts in a stated order.
Ratios that describe the same relationship.
The number used to multiply both amounts.

problems.text: The diagram has 4 red tiles and 3 blue tiles. Write red : blue. Write blue : red.
problems.case: Read a picture and preserve order
problems.worked: Name the requested first color before writing its count.

problems.text: A trail mix uses 4 raisins for every 3 nuts. How many nuts go with 12 raisins?
problems.case: Scale up by a whole number
problems.worked: Twelve is three times four, so use three times three nuts.

problems.text: A box has 20 red tiles and 15 blue tiles. Divide both counts by 5 to find an equivalent ratio.
problems.worked: Make five equal groups. Each has four red and three blue.

problems.text: A recipe uses 6 cups of oats for every 4 cups of seeds. How many cups of seeds go with 9 cups of oats?
problems.worked: Nine is 1 {1/2} times six. Multiply four by the same factor.

problems.text: Paint uses 2 cups yellow for every 5 cups blue. How much yellow goes with 15 cups blue?
problems.worked: Fifteen cups blue makes three batches. Each batch uses two cups yellow.

problems.text: Each game team has 3 builders for every 2 testers. How many builders go with 8 testers?
problems.worked: Eight testers make four groups of two. Four groups need twelve builders.

exit.text: A bracelet pattern uses 7 green beads for every 4 white beads. How many green beads go with 12 white beads?
exit.worked: Twelve white beads are three groups of four. Use three groups of seven green.
exit.error: Adding eight to each count changes the relationship.

error.text: Mia changes 4 red : 3 blue to 7 red : 6 blue by adding 3 to each count. Is the ratio unchanged?
error.correction: No. Two copies would give 8 : 6, not 7 : 6.
error.why: She uses equal additions rather than equal multiplication.
error.move: Build two full copies of the original group and compare.

example.text: A mix uses 3 cups oats for every 2 cups seeds. Find seeds for 12 cups oats.

fade.text: A mix uses 5 cups oats for every 2 cups seeds. Ten cups oats makes __ batches and needs __ cups seeds.

look_fors.response: Says four red for every three blue.
look_fors.why: Names both quantities and their order.
look_fors.move: Ask for the reversed ratio and compare meanings.

look_fors.response: Repeats or partitions a complete group.
look_fors.why: Shows equivalent ratios concretely.
look_fors.move: Ask which factor acts on both amounts.

look_fors.response: Uses a half-batch or a unit batch.
look_fors.why: Non-whole factors can preserve the ratio.
look_fors.move: Accept either method if both quantities scale equally.

misconceptions.response: Adds the same count to both colors.
misconceptions.why: Confuses additive and multiplicative change.
misconceptions.move: Build identical batches.

misconceptions.response: Says 4 : 3 means four out of three.
misconceptions.why: Confuses part-to-part and part-to-whole.
misconceptions.move: Count the total seven tiles before naming the red fraction.

discussion: Agree or disagree: Adding the same number to both counts keeps a mixture the same.
Partner compare: How do you know the recipe with nine cups of oats has the same taste?
sessions.summary_frame: To keep a ratio the same, I ___ both quantities by ___.

exit_sort.got: Gives 21 green beads and shows a factor of 3 on both quantities.
exit_sort.almost: Gives 21 with incomplete labeling, or makes a small arithmetic slip after using factor 3.
exit_sort.reteach: Gives 15 or another answer from adding the same amount.

sessions.title: Ratio tables and comparisons
sessions.goal: I can use tables, double number lines, and equal totals to solve ratio problems.
sessions.key_idea: A ratio table records equal groups. Comparing mixtures needs a common amount or a common total.
sessions.prerequisite: Scaling both amounts in a ratio.

vocab.meaning: A table of matching amounts with the same ratio.
Two aligned scales showing matching amounts.
vocab.example: Two cups concentrate matches five cups water.

vocab.meaning: A comparison between one part and the total.
vocab.example: 2 red and 3 blue makes red {2/5} of all tiles.

problems.text: Concentrate : water is 2 : 5. Complete pairs (2, 5), (4, __), and (6, 15).
problems.worked: Double both numbers in (2, 5).

diagram.caption: Each row describes the same mixture.

problems.text: For that 2 : 5 mixture, how much water matches 10 cups concentrate? Solve using a table and a double number line.
problems.case: Solve the same problem two ways
problems.worked: Table: multiply (2, 5) by five. Line: five equal jumps of 2 match five jumps of 5.

problems.text: Mix A uses 3 cups syrup to 4 cups water. Mix B uses 5 cups syrup to 8 cups water. Which has more syrup for the same water?
problems.worked: Double A to get 6 syrup : 8 water. Compare 6 syrup with 5 syrup.

problems.text: Yellow : blue paint is 2 : 3. There are 35 cups in all. How much of each color?
problems.worked: Five equal ratio parts total 35. Each part is 7 cups.

problems.text: Plot (1, 3), (2, 6), and (3, 9). Let x be bags and y be marbles. Does their straight line also pass through (0, 0)?
problems.case: Ratio points in the first quadrant
problems.worked: Each y-value is three times its x-value. Zero bags have zero marbles.

exit.text: Mix A has 4 cups juice and 3 cups water. Mix B has 6 cups juice and 5 cups water. Which has the larger fraction of juice?
exit.case: Exit: equal differences do not imply equal ratios
exit.worked: A is {4/7} juice; B is {6/11}. Compare {44/77} and {42/77}.
exit.error: Both differences are one, but the fractions of juice differ.

error.text: Leo says 2 yellow : 3 blue means {2/3} of all the paint is yellow. Repair his statement.
error.correction: There are five parts in all. Yellow is {2/5} of the paint.
error.why: He uses the other part as the whole.
error.move: Join the two yellow parts and three blue parts into one total strip.

example.text: Orange : purple tiles is 3 : 2. There are 25 tiles. Find each count.

fade.text: Green : white is 4 : 1. There are 30 beads. Five equal parts means __ beads per part. Green = __; white = __.

model.caption: Two cups concentrate pairs with five cups water.

look_fors.response: Keeps matching values in the same row.
look_fors.why: Pairs are meaningful together.
look_fors.move: Ask what one complete row means.

look_fors.response: Finds a common water amount or compares part fractions.
look_fors.why: Both are valid ratio comparisons.
look_fors.move: Accept either method and require a shared comparison unit.

look_fors.response: Adds ratio parts before using the total.
look_fors.why: Separates a part-to-part ratio from the whole.
look_fors.move: Ask the student to label all five parts.

misconceptions.why: A difference ignores mixture size.
misconceptions.move: Use the same amount of water in both mixtures.

misconceptions.response: Divides total by one ratio number.
misconceptions.why: Treats one part as the whole.
misconceptions.move: Draw and count all ratio parts first.

discussion: Agree or disagree: A mixture with more cups of juice always tastes stronger.
Partner compare: Why must the 35-cup paint total be divided into five parts?
sessions.summary_frame: To compare two mixtures fairly, I can make ___ the same.

exit_sort.got: Chooses A and compares equivalent ratios or correct fractions of juice.
exit_sort.almost: Chooses A but does not show a valid comparison, or makes a minor arithmetic slip with the right setup.
exit_sort.reteach: Says equal because the differences match, or compares only the juice counts.

bank.text: A picture shows 5 green tiles and 2 white tiles. Write green : white and white : green.
bank.worked: Keep the requested first color first.

bank.text: Is 6 : 10 equivalent to 9 : 15?
bank.worked: Multiply both numbers in 6 : 10 by one and one half.

bank.text: Ava changes 3 : 7 to 5 : 9. Is it the same ratio?
bank.worked: Adding two to each count changes the relationship. Two batches would give 6 : 14.
bank.error: Equal additions do not preserve a ratio.

bank.text: A team has 4 runners for every 3 walkers. There are 18 walkers. How many runners?
bank.worked: Eighteen walkers make six groups. Six groups need twenty-four runners.

bank.text: Red : blue is 3 : 5. How many blue tiles go with 6 red tiles?
bank.worked: The number of batches is 6 ÷ 3. Multiply that count by 5.
bank.error: Adding the same amount to both counts changes the ratio.

bank.text: Simplify the ratio 8 : 14 by dividing both counts by 2.
bank.worked: Divide both counts by the same factor.

bank.text: A recipe uses 2 cups beans for 3 cups rice. How many cups beans go with {9/2} cups rice?
bank.worked: Find the number of recipe batches by dividing the rice amount by 3. Each batch needs 2 cups beans.

bank.text: Red : blue is 3 : 5. How many blue tiles go with 9 red tiles?
bank.worked: The number of batches is 9 ÷ 3. Multiply that count by 5.
bank.error: Adding the same amount to both counts changes the ratio.

bank.text: Simplify the ratio 12 : 21 by dividing both counts by 3.
bank.worked: Divide both counts by the same factor.

bank.text: A recipe uses 2 cups beans for 3 cups rice. How many cups beans go with {15/2} cups rice?
bank.worked: Find the number of recipe batches by dividing the rice amount by 3. Each batch needs 2 cups beans.

bank.text: Red : blue is 3 : 5. How many blue tiles go with 12 red tiles?
bank.worked: The number of batches is 12 ÷ 3. Multiply that count by 5.
bank.error: Adding the same amount to both counts changes the ratio.

bank.text: Simplify the ratio 16 : 28 by dividing both counts by 4.
bank.worked: Divide both counts by the same factor.

bank.text: The pairs (2, 7), (4, 14), and (6, __) have the same ratio. Complete the table.
bank.worked: Multiply both entries of the first pair by three.

bank.text: A double number line pairs 3 minutes with 8 laps. What pairs with 12 minutes?
bank.worked: Four jumps of three minutes match four jumps of eight laps.

bank.text: Plot (1, 2), (2, 4), and (4, 8). Do they lie on a line through the origin?
bank.worked: Every vertical value is twice the horizontal value.

bank.text: A mix has 5 cups oats and 3 cups seeds. What fraction of the whole is seeds?
bank.worked: Count all eight cups before forming the fraction.
bank.error: Five counts the other part, not the whole.

bank.text: Yellow : purple is 2 : 5. There are 21 beads. Find both counts.
bank.worked: Add ratio parts: 2 + 5 = 7. Divide the total by 7, then multiply each ratio part.

bank.text: Complete the ratio-table pair: (3, 4), (9, __).
bank.worked: Multiply both entries in the first pair by the same factor.

bank.text: Mix A has 2 cups juice and 3 cups water. Mix B has 3 cups juice and 5 cups water. Which has more juice for the same water?
bank.worked: Use equivalent ratios with the same water amount, then compare juice.
bank.error: Comparing only the juice counts ignores the amount of water.

bank.text: Yellow : purple is 2 : 5. There are 28 beads. Find both counts.
bank.worked: Add ratio parts: 2 + 5 = 7. Divide the total by 7, then multiply each ratio part.

bank.text: Complete the ratio-table pair: (3, 4), (12, __).
bank.worked: Multiply both entries in the first pair by the same factor.

bank.text: Mix A has 4 cups juice and 6 cups water. Mix B has 5 cups juice and 8 cups water. Which has more juice for the same water?
bank.worked: Use equivalent ratios with the same water amount, then compare juice.
bank.error: Comparing only the juice counts ignores the amount of water.

bank.text: Yellow : purple is 2 : 5. There are 35 beads. Find both counts.
bank.worked: Add ratio parts: 2 + 5 = 7. Divide the total by 7, then multiply each ratio part.

bank.text: Complete the ratio-table pair: (3, 4), (15, __).

weeks.title: Rates and percents
weeks.big_idea: A unit rate describes an amount per one unit. Percent means per hundred. Label the whole before deciding whether to find a part, a whole, or a percent.
weeks.connections: This builds on equivalent ratios. Fraction division later extends the same grouping and scaling ideas.
weeks.omissions: Discounts, tax, and percent change wait for the optional bridge previews. Compound percent calculations are omitted.

teaser.text: A mystery number has this property: 25% of it is 6 more than 10% of it. Find the number.
teaser.worked: The gap is 15%, which equals 6. Five percent is 2, so 100% is 40.

sessions.title: Rates and unit rates
sessions.goal: I can find an amount per one unit and use it to compare rates.
sessions.key_idea: A unit rate names how much of one quantity goes with one unit of another. Its units show the division order.
sessions.prerequisite: Equivalent ratios and decimal division by whole numbers.

vocab.meaning: A ratio comparing quantities with different units.
An amount per one unit of another quantity.
For each one.
vocab.example: $0.60 per apple means $0.60 for one apple.

problems.text: A rider goes 20 kilometers in 4 hours at a steady speed. Find kilometers per hour.
problems.worked: Divide 20 kilometers by 4 hours.

problems.text: Eight apples cost $6.00. Find dollars per apple.
problems.worked: Share the total cost equally among eight apples.

problems.text: Two cups of rice make 5 servings. Find cups per serving.
problems.worked: Divide two cups among five servings. The unit is cups per serving.

problems.text: A printer makes 15 cards in 3 minutes. Find cards per minute and minutes per card.
problems.answer: 5 cards per minute; {1/5} minute per card
problems.worked: Cards per minute uses 15 ÷ 3. Minutes per card uses 3 ÷ 15.

problems.text: Pack A has 6 pencils for $2.40. Pack B has 10 pencils for $3.50. Which costs less per pencil?
problems.worked: A costs $0.40 each. B costs $0.35 each, saving $0.05 per pencil.

problems.text: A skater travels 3 miles in 20 minutes at steady speed. Find miles per hour.
problems.worked: An hour has three 20-minute groups, so multiply 3 miles by 3.

problems.text: A robot rolls 4 meters each second. Complete distances for 0, 2, and 5 seconds.
problems.worked: Multiply seconds by 4 meters per second.

exit.text: A cyclist travels 9 miles in 45 minutes at steady speed. Find miles per hour and minutes per mile.
exit.answer: 12 miles per hour; 5 minutes per mile
exit.case: Exit: two directions with time conversion
exit.worked: Nine miles in three 15-minute groups means 3 miles per 15 minutes. Four groups give 12 miles in an hour.
exit.wrong: 5 miles per hour; 12 minutes per mile
exit.error: The numbers belong to different units; label the quantity per one.

error.text: Ava says 8 apples for $6 costs {4/3} dollars per apple because 8 ÷ 6 = {4/3}. Is her unit correct?
error.correction: No. $6 ÷ 8 apples = $0.75 per apple. {4/3} describes apples per dollar.
error.move: Write dollars above the division and apples below it.

example.text: A walker travels 2 miles in 30 minutes. Find miles per hour.
steps: Two groups of 2 miles make 4 miles.
The rate is 4 miles per hour.

fade.text: A scooter travels 5 miles in 30 minutes. There are __ half-hours in one hour, so the speed is __ miles per hour.

look_fors.response: Labels dollars per apple.
look_fors.why: The units identify division order.
look_fors.move: Ask what one in the rate refers to.

look_fors.response: Uses scaling or divides to one.
look_fors.why: Both methods can find an equivalent rate.

weeks.title: Dividing fractions
weeks.big_idea: Division asks how many divisor-sized groups fit. Equal small units make the comparison visible. The reciprocal rule records that reasoning efficiently.
weeks.connections: This builds on fraction multiplication and equivalent ratios. Decimal division will also preserve group counts by renaming units.
weeks.omissions: Complex fractions, algebraic fraction equations, and lengthy multi-stage fraction contexts are omitted. Fractional prism volume is included in the Sunday session.

teaser.text: A jug holds 2 liters. You have {1/3}-liter and {1/2}-liter scoops. Use both sizes and exactly five full scoops to fill it. How many of each?
teaser.check: [(a,b) for a in range(1,5) for b in range(1,5) if a+b==5 and a*F(1,3)+b*F(1,2)==2]==[(3,2)]
teaser.worked: Try five thirds first: {5/3} liters. Replacing a third with a half adds {1/6} liter. Two replacements fill the missing third.

sessions.title: The meaning of fraction division
sessions.goal: I can show how many fractional groups fit in an amount.
sessions.key_idea: The divisor names one group. A quotient tells how many of those groups fit, even when it is part of a group.
sessions.prerequisite: Fraction equivalence and division by unit fractions.

vocab.meaning: The amount being divided.
The amount that names one group in a grouping problem.
The result of division.

problems.text: Four meters are cut into {1/5}-meter pieces. How many pieces?
problems.worked: Each meter contains five fifths. Four meters contain twenty.

problems.text: How many {2/3}-cup scoops fit in 4 cups?
problems.worked: Four cups are twelve thirds. Each scoop uses two thirds, so twelve thirds make six scoops.

problems.text: How many {1/8}-meter pieces fit in {3/4} meter?
problems.worked: Three fourths is six eighths. Count six pieces.

problems.text: How many {2/3}-cup groups fit in {5/6} cup? A fraction of a group is allowed.
problems.worked: One group is four sixths. Five sixths is five fourths of that group.

problems.text: What fraction of a {5/6}-cup scoop is filled by {1/3} cup?
problems.worked: One scoop has five sixths. One third is two sixths, so it fills two of five equal scoop parts.

problems.text: A jar is {2/3} full after {3/5} liter is poured in. How many liters fill the whole jar?
problems.case: Find amount for one whole group
problems.worked: Two thirds of the jar hold three fifths liter. One third holds three tenths, so three thirds hold nine tenths.

problems.text: Write a story for {3/4} ÷ {1/2}. Solve it.
problems.worked: Example: A pitcher has three fourths liter. How many half-liter servings does it hold, including part of a serving?

exit.text: How much of a {3/4}-meter length is {2/5} meter? Draw equal parts to show {2/5} ÷ {3/4}.
exit.case: Exit: quotient below one with different denominators
exit.worked: Use twentieths. The target length is 15 twentieths; the available amount is 8 twentieths. That is eight fifteenths of one group.
exit.error: Multiplying the two fractions finds a different amount.

error.text: Ben says {1/3} ÷ {5/6} = {5/18}. He multiplies the fractions. Explain what division asks here.
error.correction: It asks what fraction of a five-sixths group fits in one third. The answer is {2/5}.
error.why: He uses a familiar fraction rule without identifying the group.
error.move: Rename one third as two sixths and compare with five sixths.

steps: Rename one half as two fourths.

The remaining fourth is half of a two-fourths group.

look_fors.response: Renames both amounts using the same small unit.
look_fors.why: Counting comparable pieces makes division visible.
look_fors.move: Accept a tape or a number line with equal units.

look_fors.why: Avoids treating leftover units as the answer fraction.

sessions.title: Fraction division and reciprocals
sessions.goal: I can connect the reciprocal rule to equal groups and use it in measurement problems.
sessions.key_idea: Dividing by a fraction counts groups. Multiplying by its reciprocal gives the same count.
sessions.prerequisite: Fraction division with equal-part models and mixed-number conversion.

vocab.meaning: A number that multiplies with another number to make 1.
A whole number plus a fraction.
The amount of three-dimensional space a solid fills.

problems.text: Share {3/4} liter equally among 5 bottles. How much per bottle?
problems.worked: Each fourth is split into five parts, so each bottle gets three twentieths.

problems.worked: Multiply the three perpendicular edge lengths. The base area is {1/2} square meter; two layers make one cubic meter.

weeks.title: Decimals and long division
weeks.big_idea: Decimal digits name parts of a whole. Addition and subtraction combine equal place-value units. Division preserves its quotient when both quantities scale equally.
weeks.connections: This builds on whole-number operations and fraction groups. Accurate decimal arithmetic supports expressions and equations next week.
weeks.omissions: Repeating decimals and divisors producing recurring expansions are omitted. Very long multiplication and division chains are deferred to targeted boosters.

teaser.text: Use digits 2, 4, and 8 once each in the form A.BC. Which number is closest to 5?
teaser.worked: A ones digit of 4 places the number nearest 5. Among 4.28 and 4.82, the larger is nearer to 5.

sessions.title: Decimal place value and products
sessions.goal: I can add, subtract, and multiply decimals while keeping track of the value of each digit.
sessions.key_idea: Addition combines like-sized units. Multiplication combines both the number of parts and the size of each part.
sessions.prerequisite: Whole-number multiplication, regrouping, and decimal place names.

vocab.meaning: A digit’s value depends on its position.
A nearby value that helps check an answer.
One of 1,000 equal parts of a whole.

problems.worked: Write 4.700 so tenths, hundredths, and thousandths line up.
problems.error: Aligning the final digits combines different units.

problems.worked: Write 12.000. Regroup one whole into tenths, then into hundredths and thousandths.

problems.text: A rope costs $2.35 per meter. What do 4 meters cost?
problems.case: Decimal times whole number and money
problems.worked: 235 cents × 4 = 940 cents, or $9.40.

problems.text: Find 0.6 × 0.4. Is the product less than each factor?
problems.worked: Six tenths of four tenths is twenty-four hundredths.
Fifteen hundredths times two hundredths is thirty ten-thousandths, or three thousandths.

problems.text: A notebook costs $3.85 and a pen costs $1.67. You pay $10. Find the change.
problems.worked: Add costs: $5.52. Subtract from $10.00 to get $4.48.

exit.worked: 45 × 6 = 270. Hundredths times hundredths makes ten-thousandths: 0.0270. It is less than 0.06.

error.correction: Six tenths times four tenths is twenty-four hundredths, or 0.24.
error.why: He counts digits without tracking the size of the units.
error.move: Shade six tenths across and four tenths down on a hundred-square grid.

look_fors.why: Several models correctly track decimal units.

misconceptions.why: Keeps whole-number multiplication intuition.
misconceptions.move: Take a part of one shaded part of a unit square.

Partner compare: How does a grid explain the decimal point in 0.6 × 0.4?

sessions.title: Long division with decimals
sessions.goal: I can divide with decimals by preserving equal groups and checking my quotient.
sessions.key_idea: Multiplying the dividend and divisor by the same power of ten preserves the quotient.
sessions.prerequisite: Whole-number multiplication and decimal place value.

vocab.meaning: The amount left after equal groups are made.
A new dividend and divisor with the same quotient.
A division result with fractional places written in decimals.

problems.text: Use long division to find 672 ÷ 24.
problems.worked: 24 goes into 67 twice, leaving 19 tens. Bring down 2 ones. 192 ÷ 24 = 8.

problems.text: Find 27 ÷ 8. Continue into decimal places.
problems.worked: After 3 groups, 3 remains. Rename it as 30 tenths, then continue through hundredths and thousandths.

problems.text: Find 8.4 ÷ 7.
problems.worked: 84 tenths shared among 7 gives 12 tenths.

problems.text: Find 6.3 ÷ 0.09 by writing an equivalent division with a whole-number divisor.
problems.worked: Multiply both amounts by 100: 630 ÷ 9 = 70.

problems.text: Find 7 ÷ 20.
problems.worked: Seven twentieths equals thirty-five hundredths.

problems.text: A 3.6-meter ribbon is cut into 0.4-meter pieces. How many pieces?
problems.case: Divisor below one makes larger quotient
problems.worked: Rename both in tenths: 36 tenths ÷ 4 tenths = 9.

problems.text: Find 1,176 ÷ 28 and check by multiplication.
problems.worked: 28 × 40 = 1,120. Two more groups make 56, so 42 groups make 1,176.

exit.text: Find 8.4 ÷ 0.07. Write an equivalent division and check by multiplication.

exit.error: Changing only the divisor changes the quotient.
